pages.title: Finding Elements with document querySelector()
pages.content:
**1. The DOM: The Webpage's Structure**
- Every time a webpage loads, the browser instantly turns your static HTML into an organized, interactive structure called the **Document Object Model (DOM)**. 
- Imagine the DOM as a **tree** where every HTML element (``, ``, ``) is a branch or a leaf. 
- **Why it matters:** The DOM is the only way JavaScript can "see" and "touch" the elements on the page.

**DOM Tree:**
```wedce
document
│
├── 
│ ├── 
│ │ └── My Webpage
│ │
│ └── 
│ ├── Welcome!
│ ├── Click the button below:
│ └── Submit
```
**In this structure:**
- document represents the entire webpage.
- Everything else (like ``, ``, ``) lives inside it as elements you can reach and modify.
---

**2. The `document` Object: The Key**
- The `document` object is the **main, top-level key** that gives JavaScript access to the entire DOM tree. 
- It represents the whole webpage. You **must** start with `document` before you can change or interact with anything on the screen. 
- `document` ⟹ The **entry point** to your entire webpage.

---
**3. Finding Elements with `querySelector()`**
- Once you have the key (`document`), you use the `querySelector()` method to find a specific element within the page structure.

| Method | What It Does | Analogy |
|-----------------|--------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| `querySelector()` | Finds and returns the very first element that matches the given selector. | Like searching for the first "blue car" on a street. |

**Using CSS Selectors**
- The magic of `querySelector()` is that it uses the exact CSS selectors you already know to target elements:

| To find... | Use this Selector | Example |
|------------------|--------------------|----------------------------------|
| An ID | The `#` symbol | `document.querySelector('#main-title');` |
| A Class | The `.` symbol | `document.querySelector('.primary-button');` |
| A Paragraph	 |The tag name (p)	| `document.querySelector('p');`|

---
**The Syntax for Selecting Elements**
- After you select an element, you typically store it in a variable so you can work with it later. The general syntax looks like this:
```Js
// Selects the first element matching the CSS selector
const variableName = document.querySelector('your-css-selector');
```
**Now that you understand how to find elements, let's look at a practical example to see these concepts in action!**

pages.title: Selecting Multiple Elements - querySelectorAll()
pages.content:
**The Problem with `querySelector()`**
- In the last lesson, we learned that `document.querySelector('.item')` will **only find the very first** element that matches the selector. 
- But what if you have a shopping list, a navigation menu, or several cards, and you need to interact with **all** of them? 
- You need a way to grab an entire group at once.

---
**Meet `querySelectorAll()`**
- The solution is `document.querySelectorAll()`.
- It works almost exactly like `querySelector()`, using the same CSS selectors (`.class`, `#id`, `tag`), but with one key difference:

| Method | What It Returns | Analogy |
|-------------------|-----------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------|
| `querySelector()` | One single element (the first match). | Finding one specific house number. |
| `querySelectorAll()`|A list of all elements that match the selector.| Finding all houses on a street with the same blue paint.|

---
**The NodeList: The Resulting List**
- When you use `querySelectorAll()`, the result is **not a single element**; it's a special type of list called a **NodeList**.
- A NodeList is like a collection or an array that holds all the HTML elements your selector found.
 - If your selector matches 5 list items, your NodeList will contain those 5 items.
 - If your selector matches zero items, the NodeList will be empty (but it won't crash your code!).

**Syntax**
```js
// This will find ALL elements with the class 'product-card'
const allProducts = document.querySelectorAll('.product-card');

// 'allProducts' now holds a NodeList containing all the matching elements.
```

pages.title: Two Types of DOM Results
pages.content:
- When you use JavaScript to find elements, the result you get back falls into one of two categories. The type of result dictates how you can interact with it.

| Result Type | Method Used | Analogy |
|-----------------|---------------------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| Single Element | document.querySelector() | Finding a single key. |
| NodeList | document.querySelectorAll() | Finding a keyring with multiple keys. |

---
**1. The Single Element (The Individual Key)**
- When you use `querySelector()`, the result is a direct reference to **one HTML element**.
- **How you use it:** You can immediately change its properties.

**Example:** 
If you save the heading to a variable named `title`, you can change it directly:
```js
title.textContent = "New Title"; // Works immediately!
```
---
**2. The NodeList (The Keyring Collection)**\
When you use `querySelectorAll()`, the result is a **NodeList**. This is a special collection that looks like an array but is not exactly an array (we'll cover that difference later!).
- **What it is:** A numbered list of HTML elements (or nodes) found by your selector.
- **How you use it:** You **cannot** change the properties of the entire list at once.
 - Access a specific item by its position (index), like `[0]`.
 - Use a `for` loop to iterate through the list one item at a time.
---
**The Key Difference in Practice**
- If you try to change the text content of the entire NodeList, it fails because the NodeList itself doesn't have a `textContent` property—only the individual elements inside it do!

| Code | Result | Reason |
|---------------------------------- |------------|---------------------------------|
| singleElement.textContent = "Hi"; | SUCCESS! | You are talking to one element. |
| nodeList.textContent = "Hi"; | FAIL! | You are talking to a list, not an element. |

pages.title: Selecting Elements in JavaScript
pages.content:
**Why Learn the Old Ways?**\
You already know the best tools (`querySelector` and `querySelectorAll`). So why learn these older methods?

- **Read Legacy Code:** You will often encounter code written years ago that uses these methods. You need to understand them to read and update that code.
- **Special Cases:** For selecting by ID, the classic way is still technically the fastest method the browser offers.
- These methods pre-date the modern `querySelector` functions.

---
**1. `document.getElementById()`**
- This is the simplest, most direct way to select a single element based on its unique ID.
- **Syntax:** You only pass the ID name, *without* the `#` symbol.
- **Result:** It always returns a **Single Element** (or `null` if not found).

| Method | Selector Used | Result Type | Example Code |
|-------------------|---------------------------|----------------|-------------------------------------|
| `getElementById()` | Just the ID name (no `#`) | Single Element | `document.getElementById('profile-name');` |

---
**2. `document.getElementsByClassName()`**

- This method selects **all** elements that share a specific class name.
- **Syntax:** You pass the class name, *without* the `.` symbol.
- **Result:** It returns an **HTMLCollection**.

---
**HTMLCollection vs. NodeList**
- **HTMLCollection:** A live collection of **only element nodes** (e.g., ``, ``).
- **NodeList:** A (usually static) collection that can contain element nodes, text nodes, and other node types.

- **Live Collection:** If new elements are added to the page *after* you run the code, an **HTMLCollection** automatically updates to include them. A **NodeList** often does not.

| Method | Selector Used | Result Type | Example Code |
|---------------------------|----------------------------|-----------------|-----------------------------------------------|
| `getElementsByClassName()` | Just the class name (no `.`) | HTMLCollection | `document.getElementsByClassName('data-point');` |

practiceProblems.title: DOM Selection Techniques - Worked Example
practiceProblems.description:
This example shows how to select and update both single and multiple elements using JavaScript's classic DOM selection methods.

---
**Select the Header by ID**
```js
const headerDiv = document.getElementById('header');
headerDiv.querySelector('h1').textContent = "Selectors Learned!";
```
* `getElementById('header')` finds the element with the unique ID "header".
* Since IDs are unique, this always returns a single element.
* We then use `querySelector('h1')` inside it to select the heading and change its text.

**Select All Items by Class Name**
```js
const topics = document.getElementsByClassName('topic');
```

pages.title: Changing Text - Using textContent
pages.content:
- The whole point of JavaScript and the DOM is to make your webpage interactive and dynamic. The very first way you do this is by **changing the text** that users see on the screen. 
- The property you use to read or change the text inside any HTML element is **textContent**.
- Every HTML element you select - whether it's an ``, a ``, or a `` - has a built-in property called `textContent`.

**Reading Text (Getting Information)**
- You can use `textContent` to read the current text of an element and save it to a variable.
```js
const myHeading = document.querySelector('h1');

// READ: Get the current text and store it.
const currentText = myHeading.textContent;

console.log(currentText); // Output: Whatever the h1 currently says
```

**Writing Text (Setting Information)**
- This is where the magic happens! To change the text, you simply treat the property like a variable and assign it a new string value using the equals sign (=).
```js
const button = document.querySelector('#action-btn');

// WRITE: Overwrite the existing text with a new string.
button.textContent = "I was just clicked!";
```
---
**Key Concept: Selection First!**
- You **must** successfully select an element before you can use the `.textContent` property on it. 
Remember the two steps:

- **Select** the element (e.g., using `querySelector`)
- **Modify** the element (e.g., using `.textContent`)

pages.title: Changing HTML Structure - innerHTML
pages.content:
You know that `textContent` is great for changing simple text. But what if you want to:
* Add a new button inside a container?
* Turn plain text into a clickable link?
* Add a styled list of items?

For these tasks, you need a property that understands HTML tags: `innerHTML`.

---
**1. What is `innerHTML`?**
- The `innerHTML` property allows you to read or write the entire HTML content inside an element.
* **Definition:** It returns the element's content, including all nested HTML tags, as a single string.
* **Best Use:** Injecting new, complex elements (like a ``, ``, or ``) into the DOM.

**2. The Power of Injection**
- Unlike `textContent`, which displays tags as literal text, `innerHTML` tells the browser to render (or create) the actual HTML structure.

```javascript
const box = document.querySelector('#container');

// This code injects a new, active HTML element!
box.innerHTML = 'New Section TitleClick here.';
```
 - querySelector('#container') finds the element with the ID container.
 - innerHTML replaces its content with new HTML.
 - The text between quotes creates a heading, a paragraph, and a clickable link.
 - The browser reads this string and renders real HTML elements, not just text.

pages.title: Changing Appearance - style Property
pages.content:
You already know CSS is the main tool for styling. But sometimes, you need styles to change dynamically based on a user's action:
* When a user clicks a button, the text turns red.
* When a score drops, the background color turns yellow as a warning.\
JavaScript achieves this using the `.style` property.

---
**1. The `.style` Property**
- Every HTML element you select has a `.style` property attached to it. This property is your direct bridge to controlling that element's CSS.
- Think of `.style` as a mini-CSS object built into every element.

**2. The Syntax Rule: CamelCase**
- The biggest difference when setting styles in JavaScript is that you cannot use the dashes (`-`) found in CSS properties (like `background-color`).
- Instead, you must convert the CSS name to camelCase:

| CSS Property | JavaScript `.style` Property |
|--------------|------------------------------|
| `background-color` | `backgroundColor` |
| `font-size` | `fontSize` |
| `border-radius` | `borderRadius` |

**3. Applying a Style**
- The workflow is: **Select Element → Access `.style` → Set Property → Assign Value (as a string)**.
```javascript
const box = document.querySelector('#warning-box');

// Set the CSS property directly on the element's style object.
box.style.backgroundColor = 'red'; 
box.style.fontSize = '20px';
```
---
**Key Note: Value is a String!**
- The value you assign to the style property must always be a string (inside single or double quotes), just like in your CSS file. Even numbers need a unit:

* Correct: `element.style.padding = '10px';`
* Incorrect: `element.style.padding = 10;`
---
**A Small Caution**
- `.style` only changes inline styles - not the rules written in `external` or `internal CSS` files.
- If you need to apply or remove multiple style rules together, it’s better to use `CSS classes` (we’ll learn that later).

pages.title: Switching CSS Classes with classList
pages.content:
You've seen how the `.style` property can change things like color or font size. It works - but it quickly becomes messy and repetitive:
* Adds inline styles directly into HTML (breaks clean CSS separation)
* Needs multiple lines of JS for multiple style changes

The smarter way: let your CSS handle the styling, and let JavaScript simply switch classes using `classList`.

---
**1. The Power of `classList`**
- The `classList` property gives you full control over an element's CSS classes. Think of it as a toolkit for adding, removing, or toggling class names easily.

| Method | What It Does | Analogy |
|--------|--------------|---------|
| `.add('className')` | Adds a new class | Putting a "Warning" sticker on the box |
| `.remove('className')` | Removes an existing class | Taking the sticker off |
| `.toggle('className')` | Adds if missing, removes if present | The perfect ON/OFF switch |
| `.contains('className')` | Checks if a class exists | "Does this box have the sticker?" |

**2.The Core Workflow (CSS → JS)**
- The entire process should always start in your CSS file:

1. **Define the Look (CSS):** Create a CSS class (e.g., `.highlight` or `.error`) that holds all the style changes (color, background, border, etc.).
2. **Control the Class (JavaScript):** Use the `classList` methods to simply add, remove, or check for that pre-defined class.

3. **Syntax**
```javascript
// Step 1: Select the element
const card = document.querySelector('#card');

// Step 2: Add a new class
card.classList.add('active'); // Adds the 'active' class

// Step 3: Remove a class
card.classList.remove('hidden'); // Removes the 'hidden' class

// Step 4: Toggle a class
card.classList.toggle('highlight'); // Adds or removes 'highlight' each time

```

practiceProblems.title: Toggling Classes with classList
practiceProblems.description:
This example shows how JavaScript can dynamically change an element's appearance by swapping pre-defined CSS classes using the `classList` property.

**How the Code Works**

**1. Select and Check the Status**
- The script first selects the target card (`#status-card`). Then, it immediately uses `classList.contains('default')` to check the card's current appearance state.
```javascript
const statusCard = document.querySelector('#status-card');
const isDefault = statusCard.classList.contains('default');
```
**2. Decision and Removal**
- Because the card starts with `class="default"` in the HTML, the `isDefault` variable is `true`. The `if` statement runs, and the code immediately uses `classList.remove('default')`. This instantly strips away the gray background and styles defined by the `.default` rule in the external CSS file.
```javascript
statusCard.classList.remove('default');
```
**3. Addition and Visual Update**
- Next, the script uses `classList.add('alert')`. This applies all the styles defined in the `.alert` CSS rule (red background, dark text, border) to the element. Since all styling is handled by the CSS, the change is clean, fast, and visual.
```javascript
statusCard.classList.add('alert');
statusCard.textContent = "Current Status: ALERT! ";
```
---
**Your Challenge**
- Task : Add an Immediate Toggle: Inside the if block in `script.js`, after the `statusCard.classList.add('alert');` line, add `statusCard.classList.toggle('alert');`.

practiceProblems.title: Interactive Profile Card
practiceProblems.description:
In this mini-project, you'll create a dynamic profile card that updates its content, style, and theme using JavaScript.

**What You'll Learn**

* Select elements using `querySelector()` and `querySelectorAll()`
* Change text with `textContent` and `innerHTML`
* Style elements with `.style`
* Switch themes using `.classList.toggle()`

---
**Phases of Development**

**Phase 1 – Selecting Elements**
- Learn how to select elements from the page using `querySelector()` and `querySelectorAll()`. You'll select the name, bio, theme, and the card itself, and see how multiple elements can be selected at once.

**Phase 2 – Changing Text & HTML**
- Update the profile's name and bio using `.textContent`. Then modify the theme label using `.innerHTML` to include an emoji and new text. This shows how you can change content dynamically.

**Phase 3 – Styling & Toggling Theme**
- Change the card's style dynamically using `.style` (background color, border, scale). Then apply a Fun Mode theme using `.classList.toggle()` to switch CSS classes. This shows how styles and themes can transform the card visually.

practiceProblems.title: Styling & Theme Switching
practiceProblems.description:
**Goal:** Improve the look of your profile card and add a theme change effect using JavaScript styling and class toggling.

**Instructions**
1. Open your `script.js` file. 
 - Continue using the same card element you selected in earlier phases. 
2. Apply direct style changes to the card using the `.style` property. 
 - Change the background color of the card to a light pink shade. 
 - Add a solid border around the card to make it stand out. 
 - Slightly scale up the card to make it look more prominent on the page. 
 - These updates should immediately make your profile card more lively and visually engaging. 
3. Next, add a **theme toggle** effect using `.classList.toggle()`. 
 - In your JavaScript, use `.classList.toggle("fun-mode")` on the card element to apply or remove this theme. 
 - When you run your code, you’ll see the card smoothly switch between normal mode and fun mode. 

---
**What Happens on the Page**
- The card’s background color, border, and size change instantly through JavaScript. 
- When the `fun-mode` class is toggled, the card’s theme updates to a more colorful version. 

This shows how JavaScript can control both direct style updates and complete theme changes.
